job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

response.passage: Last Tuesday, our science teacher, Mrs. Iyer, brought 45 fresh onion bulbs to our classroom in Bengaluru. She wanted us to observe how tiny, repeating units called cells work together to form tissues. We carefully peeled the thin, transparent skin from the onion layers. Rohan, who sat in the front row, noticed that the skin looked like a brick wall under the microscope. Mrs. Iyer explained that these cells are organized into layers because they need to provide structural support to the plant. Later, Priya accidentally dropped 3 slides on the floor, but we managed to finish the experiment. We learned that just as bricks build a house, these microscopic cells build the tissues that keep the onion firm. The activity showed us that tissues are not just random collections, but organized groups performing specific jobs. By the end of the day, we understood that the onion's strength comes from this orderly arrangement of cells. It was fascinating to see how something so small could be so complex.
response.summary: Students in Bengaluru observed onion skin under a microscope to understand how cells form tissues. They learned that organized cell structures provide necessary support and strength to the plant.
